chunks: The Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him) said to Shurayh: 'Do not whisper privately to anyone in your gathering, and if you become angry, then arise, and do not issue a judgment while you are angry.'

He (the narrator) said: And Abu Abdillah (blessings of God be upon him) said: 'The tongue of a judge is behind his heart — if it is in his favor, he speaks; and if it is against him, he remains silent.'

key_terms.تُسَارَّ: To whisper secretly, to confer privately — prohibited in judicial settings as it breeds suspicion
key_terms.غَضْبَان: Angry, wrathful — state which disqualifies a judge from issuing rulings
key_terms.لِسَانُ الْقَاضِي وَرَاءَ قَلْبِهِ: The tongue of the judge is behind his heart — the judge's speech must follow his reasoned discernment
key_terms.مَجْلِس: Gathering, court session — the formal setting for adjudication

ai.seo_question: What did Imam Ali say about judicial conduct and issuing judgments while angry?
ai.summary: This hadith transmits two complementary teachings on judicial ethics. The first, from Imam Ali (peace be upon him) to Shurayh ibn al-Harith al-Kindi — a judge appointed during the early Islamic era — prohibits private whispering in court sessions (which could create suspicion of bias or corruption) and forbids passing judgments while in a state of anger (which clouds reason). The second saying, from Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him), uses a vivid metaphor: the judge's tongue should be subordinate to his heart's discernment, speaking only when the truth is clear and favorable, and remaining silent when doubt or partiality might distort his ruling.
